items.followUp: Differentiate between an atom and a molecule.

rubric.why: A molecule is neutral and consists of two or more chemically bonded atoms.
rubric.description: Defines a molecule as a neutral group of bonded atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a molecule is neutral and 1 mark for stating that it consists of bonded atoms.

rubric.why: A molecular ion is a group of bonded atoms with an overall positive or negative charge.
rubric.description: Identifies a molecular ion as a bonded group of atoms with an overall charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is charged and 1 mark for identifying it as a group of bonded atoms.

modelAnswer: A molecule is an electrically neutral group of two or more atoms chemically bonded together.
A molecular ion is a group of two or more bonded atoms that carries an overall positive or negative charge.
For example, NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻ are molecular ions.

items.followUp: Define a coordinate covalent bond and explain its formation in the ammonium ion.

rubric.why: A coordinate covalent bond has a shared pair of electrons supplied entirely by one atom.
rubric.description: Defines a coordinate covalent bond by the shared electron pair and its single-atom donor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the shared pair of electrons and 1 mark for stating that one atom donates both electrons.

rubric.why: In forming ammonium, ammonia donates a lone pair to a hydrogen ion, forming NH₄⁺.
rubric.description: Explains the ammonium-ion example, including the donor, acceptor and product.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying ammonia/NH₃ as the donor and H⁺ as the acceptor, and 1 mark for giving NH₄⁺ as the product.

rubric.why: Water donates a lone pair to a hydrogen ion to form the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺.
rubric.description: Gives the hydronium-ion example of coordinate bond formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water/H₂O and H⁺ as forming H₃O⁺.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by one atom.
Ammonia (NH₃) donates a lone pair from nitrogen to a hydrogen ion (H⁺), forming the ammonium ion (NH₄⁺).
Water (H₂O) donates a lone pair from oxygen to a hydrogen ion (H⁺), forming the hydronium ion (H₃O⁺).
An arrow may be used to show the direction of donation, from the donor atom to the acceptor.

items.followUp: Explain how cations and anions are formed.

rubric.why: A cation is positively charged because it loses one or more electrons.
rubric.description: Identifies a cation as a positive ion formed by loss of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both the positive charge and loss of electrons.

rubric.why: An anion is negatively charged because it gains one or more electrons.
rubric.description: Identifies an anion as a negative ion formed by gain of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both the negative charge and gain of electrons.

modelAnswer: A cation is a positively charged ion formed when an atom loses one or more electrons.
An anion is a negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains one or more electrons.

items.followUp: Define atomic number and mass number, and give an example of isotopes.

rubric.why: Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers because they have different numbers of neutrons.
rubric.description: Defines isotopes using their shared atomic number and differing mass numbers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both defining features, or for stating the same proton number and different neutron numbers.

rubric.why: A correct pair of isotopes illustrates the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of isotopes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct isotope pair, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14.

modelAnswer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
For example, carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon.
